intro.title: Node.js
intro.intro: Every question here starts BROKEN, not correct — read the intended behavior, find the bug, and fix it in the editor on the left. Click Run to check your fix against the given test cases for real (it actually executes your code, in your own browser, sandboxed in a Web Worker with a timeout — an infinite loop just times out instead of freezing anything). Once your fix passes the given cases, call the function one more time with the input the question asks for, and submit that result as the flag.

questions.title: One Off the End

hints.text: Trace `sumRange(3, 3)` by hand against the loop condition `i < b`. Does the loop body ever run at all?
The loop must include `b` itself. Change the comparison so the last iteration is `i === b`, not one before it.

questions.title: Same Shape, Different Boxes
questions.description:
`isSame(a, b)` should return `true` when two arrays hold the same values in the same order — a **value** comparison, not a reference comparison.

```js
function isSame(a, b) {
  return a === b;
}
```

`===` on two arrays checks whether they are literally the same object in memory, which is almost never what `[1,2,3]` built twice actually is.

Run checks:

- `isSame([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])` should be `true`
- `isSame([1, 2], [1, 2, 3])` should be `false`

Once both pass, submit the results of these three calls with your fix, joined by underscores, as `CTF{r1_r2_r3}`:

- `isSame([1], [1])`
- `isSame([1, 2], [2, 1])`
- `isSame([], [])`

hints.text: Two arrays are equal in VALUE when they have the same length and every element at the same index matches — nothing to do with whether they're the same object.
`a.length === b.length && a.every((v, i) => v === b[i])` is the whole fix.

questions.title: Backwards, With Gaps

hints.text: `.split('').reverse()` is already correct — the bug is entirely in how the pieces are put back together.
`.join(' ')` inserts a space between every character. You want no separator at all: `.join('')`.

questions.title: Multiplying by Nothing

hints.text: Trace `factorial(2)`: it calls `factorial(1)`, which calls `factorial(0)`. Whatever `factorial(0)` returns gets multiplied into every step above it.
The base case — what an empty product equals — has to be `1`, not `0`. Multiplying anything by `0` at the bottom of the recursion zeroes out the whole chain.

questions.title: The Seed That Wasn't Zero

hints.text: `reduce`'s second argument is the STARTING value of the accumulator — check what it's seeded with before any element has been added.
Summing should start from `0`, not `1`. That trailing `1` in the reduce call is the whole bug.

questions.title: Ten Sorts Before Two
questions.description:
`sortAscending(nums)` should sort an array of numbers into ascending numeric order.

```js
function sortAscending(nums) {
  return nums.sort();
}
```

`Array.prototype.sort()` with no arguments compares elements as STRINGS by default — so `10` sorts before `2`, because `"1"` comes before `"2"`.

Run checks:

- `sortAscending([10, 1, 2])` should be `[1, 2, 10]`
- `sortAscending([40, 5, 100, 25])` should be `[5, 25, 40, 100]`

Once both pass, run your fixed `sortAscending([9, 80, 7, 15])` and submit the four results in order as `CTF{a_b_c_d}`.

hints.text: `sort()` needs a comparator function to sort numbers numerically — without one, it converts everything to a string first.
`nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)` — a negative result means `a` comes first, which is exactly numeric ascending order.

questions.title: Every Counter Remembers the Same Number

hints.text: `var` is function-scoped, not block-scoped — there is only ONE `i` for the entire loop, and every closure created inside the loop shares that same one variable.
Changing `var i` to `let i` gives each iteration of the loop its own fresh binding of `i`, which is what each closure needs to capture.

questions.title: The Copy That Wasn't

hints.text: A spread (`{ ...user }`) is a SHALLOW copy — nested objects and arrays inside it are shared by reference with the original, not duplicated.
The `address` field needs its own copy too: `{ ...user, address: { ...user.address } }`.

questions.title: One Level, Not All of Them

hints.text: `.flat(Infinity)` flattens every level of nesting, all the way down — the question only ever asked for one level.
`.flat(1)` (or just `.flat()`, whose default depth is `1`) is the fix.

questions.title: Whose `this` Is It Anyway

hints.text: A regular `function` passed as a callback does not inherit `this` from where it was written — only from how IT is called, and `.map` calls it plainly, with no receiver.

An ARROW function has no `this` of its own — it lexically inherits `this` from `getValueTimes`, which IS `obj` when called as `obj.getValueTimes(...)`. Replace the callback with `(f) => this.value * f`.
